content.text: The JSONL confirms the weekly limit interrupted three active follow-up jobs. I’m checking each job’s last recorded actions against its worktree so I can distinguish finished PRs from partial work.

Yes. I found the [local Claude JSONL session](</Users/gabe/.claude/projects/-Users-gabe-Projects-caliper--claude-worktrees-release-0-2-0/ba6a68d6-c702-4382-ab2f-60cd0f6af675.jsonl>). The last substantive request was to find a good speed and memory setting for lazy sessions and close more of the prop type gap using structural fixes and, where needed, TypeScript 7.1.

Claude had three jobs running when the weekly limit stopped them:

- **Lazy session performance:** A threshold sweep had run, and work on a chained dependency index was underway in `perf/chained-layer-index`. The worktree has uncommitted code and pending snapshot files.
- **Confidence scoring:** An oracle analysis script was written in `chore/confidence-score`, but the agent found a join bug and was fixing and rerunning the analysis. Its results are not ready to use.
- **Prop gap:** The agent traced 5,544 of shadcn’s 7,499 missing props to one `@react-types/shared` declaration file and was inspecting React Aria wrappers when it stopped. That investigation is unfinished.

The related completed work is in open PRs [#200](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/200), [#201](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/201), and [#202](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/202). All checks on #202 have since passed. The main checkout is clean but behind `origin/main`; the unfinished work is in separate worktrees. I haven’t changed any files.

This was the last bit in the UI:

PR #202 makes dependency loading the default, and 15 of its 16 checks pass. The one pending job is the non-blocking Equivalence check. The fork couldn't watch CI itself because its worktree was deleted partway through.

What changed
- Default: PipelineOptions::load_dependencies is true. The CLI has --no-load-dependencies on extract, inspect, watch and check, and --load-dependencies is still accepted as a no-op alias. The two flags conflict, and a flag overrides the config.
- Other surfaces: the NAPI, Vite plugin and addon docs and types say on by default, with loadDependencies: false to opt out.
- Docs: ADR 0019 (it supersedes 0010's "off by default"), the ADR index, README, STATUS, parity.md and a minor changeset.
- Pinned to the old behaviour on purpose: the corpus snapshot tests (with it on, the Mantine and Chakra snapshots changed because the installed csstype turns string props into literal unions), apps/validate/src/run-ours.ts, and scripts/parity.py, which passes --no-load-dependencies only to builds that know the flag.

- Chakra is 4.4× slower and holds 3.3× the memory by default. shadcn takes 40 ms and 124 MiB more. The other three take 10–20 ms and 16–25 MiB more.
- Against RDT's props (from the 0.4.0 baseline, not re-measured): Chakra 0.1% → 98.6%, shadcn 6.4% → 39.5%, antd 71.8% → 80.3%.
- Without node_modules: same props and unresolved count, 40 ms on against 30 ms off, no crash. Monorepos (Mantine, Chakra, Spectrum) ran without error.

+# 0020. Chain dependency layers and load the remaining names after three growths
+
+**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-25 **Supersedes:** the 48-growth threshold and full-layer rebuild in [0016](0016-resolve-components-on-request.md)
+
+## Context
+
+ADR 0016 made each growth share the project's indexes, but `dependency_types::load` still rebuilt its own index from every dependency file the session had loaded. After 48 growths it loaded the remaining names in the background to avoid more rebuilds. On shadcn, 50 requests then took 106 ms and held 94 MiB; loading the remaining names after three growths cut the time to about 61 ms but held about 148 MiB. The speed of a static Storybook build matters more than that memory difference, provided answers remain equal to batch extraction.
+
+## Decision
+
+Each growth holds only the declarations and lookup answers it adds, with an `Arc` to the previous layer. Type and import lookups follow the chain. A file parsed earlier as a re-export stub is indexed when a later demand first claims a declaration in it. After eight links, the next growth flattens the chain so lookup depth stays bounded. A lazy session starts loading the rest of the project's dependency names in the background after its third growth.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- At the three-growth threshold, 50 seeded requests are faster than the previous full-layer implementation on every installed corpus: Mantine 42 → 30 ms, Chakra 313 → 234 ms, shadcn 61 → 52 ms, antd 23 → 18 ms, Spectrum 27 → 20 ms. Peak RSS falls or stays close to the previous three-growth run: shadcn 148 → 144 MB. These are best-of-three process measurements with the same corpus and output digest.
+- Against the chained implementation at 48 growths, three growths make shadcn's 50 requests 52 instead of 72 ms and its whole-project read 213 instead of 272 ms. The 50-request peak is 144 instead of 94 MB. antd's whole-project read is 56 instead of 126 ms with 81 instead of 84 MB. The other corpora also improve in time; the full table is in `docs/performance.md`.
+- All ten workload digests match the prior build. `lazy_parity` matches batch entries and diagnostics over all five installed corpora when components are requested together, forward one at a time, and reverse one at a time. Flattening and a stub claimed later have direct regression tests.
+- Watch revisions can keep adding layers. Flattening copies the accumulated layer once per nine growths; a growth that does not flatten processes only newly claimed files.
+
+## Alternative considered
+
+Keep the 48-growth threshold: it saves about 50 MB on shadcn's 50-request sample but makes the whole-project reads slower on all five corpora.

Yes. I picked up the interrupted work in separate worktrees and ran an adversarial check. **Nothing has been committed, pushed, or merged.**

- **Chained dependency loader:** I found and fixed a correctness bug when a file first parsed as a re-export stub was later needed for its declarations. I added a regression test and forward-order lazy parity coverage. The core library tests passed (639 tests), as did clippy and five-corpus lazy parity. The local threshold sweep produced identical output digests at both settings; the faster setting uses more memory on shadcn.
- **Confidence experiment:** Claude’s initial labels covered only props both tools reported, so they could not measure missing props. I added checker-only prop labels and separated large inherited layers that Caliper deliberately summarizes. The analysis has just **one “wrong type” example** across six corpora; that is too little evidence to use the score for automatic fallback.
- **Semantic gap:** TypeScript sees a `tw` prop on 1,154 shadcn components through Next’s React `HTMLAttributes` module augmentation. Caliper does not apply that augmentation. This accounts for a substantial part of the remaining checker-only props and needs a separate design decision.
- **PR #202:** All 16 checks now pass. Its architecture documentation still describes dependency loading as off by default, so that text needs updating before merge.

The loader work is in [the chained-layer worktree](/Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/agent-acbb81e8b835c4e39), and the oracle analysis is in [the confidence worktree](/Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/agent-a9a3030cd4e625228). The full snapshot suite in the loader worktree remains unverified: seven snapshots differ in absolute path prefixes because that worktree resolves `node_modules` through the main checkout. I would address that test setup, then review the module-augmentation gap before proposing a merge order.

content.text:
The **chained dependency loader** is ready for a commit and a PR stacked on **#200**. I staged its 11 code, test, and documentation files. The generated `.snap.new` files are excluded.

Proposed commit message:

```text
perf: chain lazy dependency layers

Avoid reindexing every loaded dependency on each growth so a session can load the remaining names after three growths.
```

Proposed PR: **“perf: chain lazy dependency layers”** → base `perf/shared-index-on-growth` in `orin-dx/caliper`.

PR body:

```markdown
## Summary
- Keep each dependency growth in a bounded chain and flatten after eight links.
- Load the remaining project names after three growths.
- Index a file when it is first claimed as a declaration, even if an earlier layer parsed it as a re-export stub.

## Verification
- Core library tests: 639 passed; clippy and formatting passed.
- Lazy parity passed on five installed corpora in batch, forward, and reverse request order.
- All ten benchmark output digests matched the prior build. The three-growth chain improved whole-project time on all five corpora; shadcn's 50-request peak rose from 94 to 144 MB compared with a 48-growth threshold.

## Limitation
The local full snapshot run had seven absolute-path-prefix differences because this worktree resolves node_modules through the main checkout.
```

The confidence experiment is still research work; I would leave it out of this PR. The **courier:commit** and **courier:pr** skills require approval of the exact message, scope, and PR draft before committing or creating a PR. **Approve this commit and stacked PR as drafted?**
Create it and start the next piece of work
I’ll create the approved commit and stacked PR, then move to the next piece: separating real prop omissions from intentional collapsing in the confidence and prop-gap work.

content.text: I found a concrete cause for 1,408 of the shadcn checker-only props: wrappers such as `TabsTrigger` use `ComponentProps<typeof TabPrimitive>`, where `TabPrimitive` is an imported `declare const` with a callable type. Caliper records a warning but does not recognize that declaration as a component. I’m adding a narrow regression case for that declaration shape before changing the extractor.

*** Add File: /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/agent-a9a3030cd4e625228/docs/confidence-experiment.md
+# Confidence routing experiment
+
+The score uses only Caliper's emitted prop shapes, component metadata, and diagnostics. TypeScript 7.1 supplies offline labels for evaluation. A production score would not require the TypeScript 7.1 opt-in; invoking the semantic backend for a routed component would still be an explicit product decision.
+
+## Result on the pinned corpora
+
+Measured on 2026-10-25 with the structural binary at `3f20f965` and its PR stack, `typescript@7.1.0-beta`, and the five corpora in `scripts/parity.py` plus fixtures. The checker and Caliper share 518,041 labelled props. The oracle marks one prop `wrong`: `RouterProvider.navigate` in Spectrum. Its source preserves `Href` and `RouterOptions` aliases; the checker instantiates the unaugmented `RouterConfig` to `string` and `undefined`. This is a spelling and environment difference, not evidence of a consumer-visible incorrect function signature. One hard label cannot validate an automatic fallback rule.
+
+| Target at 10% of matched components routed | Existing warning rule | Smoothed table | Logistic model |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| Shared `wrong` or `less precise` props, five-corpus mean | 10% | 27% | 25% |
+| Checker-only props outside summarized layers, five-corpus mean | 24% | 3% | 8% |
+
+The soft label includes many type spellings that may be useful to preserve in RDT-compatible output. The table and model catch no hard `wrong` labels at a 20% component budget. Routing individual props has the same missing-prop blind spot: a prop that Caliper never emitted has no prop-level score.
+
+## Missing props
+
+The checker reports 1,182 props absent from matched shadcn components after excluding props attributed to intentionally summarized inheritance layers. Of these, 1,154 originate in Next's ambient augmentation, 22 in the TypeScript DOM library, and 6 in Radix Menubar. The other corpora have 27 antd, 12 Chakra, 67 Mantine, 52 Spectrum, and 13 fixture missing props by the same heuristic. The matching procedure does not evaluate components the checker finds but Caliper does not match.
+
+These are separate coverage labels, not `wrong` type labels. The layer exclusion matches declaration paths, so it can misclassify a prop when different types share one file. A routing policy trained on these labels would mostly learn package augmentation and corpus composition rather than structural extraction risk.
+
+## Reproduce
+
+After `scripts/parity.py setup` has installed the pinned corpora and `cargo build --release` has built the CLI:
+
+```bash
+python3 scripts/parity.py oracle --bin target/release/caliper-docgen --corpora .parity/corpora --work .parity/confidence-oracle
+python3 scripts/confidence.py --work .parity/confidence-oracle --out .parity/confidence-report.md
+```
+
+`oracle` writes every shared-prop verdict, the checker-only and summarized prop rows, and their declaration paths. `confidence.py` evaluates a warning rule, a smoothed table, and a logistic model with leave-one-corpus-out fitting and equal corpus weight. The script reports both component and prop budgets, and keeps the one hard `wrong` label visible.
+
+No automatic checker routing follows from this experiment. Continue fixing reachable structural gaps and measuring missing props separately from shared-prop type disagreements.
*** End Patch";

I continued the hardening work and opened [PR #210](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/210), stacked on #209. An exact dependency test exposed a generic namespace component prop emitted as `T`; the fix emits `unknown`, matching direct `ComponentProps<typeof Component>` resolution. All 640 core unit tests pass, Clippy is clean, and the five pinned corpora are byte identical to #209 in both dependency-loading configurations.

I also corrected [PR #208’s confidence experiment](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/208). Its missing-prop labels now exclude intentionally omitted `ref`/`key` props, skip ambiguous duplicate display names, and match export names by case. A full oracle rerun produced **518,268 labelled shared props and one `wrong` label**. At a 10% component budget, the score still catches only **6% of missing props**; this does not support automatic checker routing. All 16 CI checks pass on each PR from **#204 through #210**.

**The broader gap work is still open.** The corrected inventory includes Mantine’s 66 missing props through local generic aliases, Chakra’s 12 recipe props, antd’s 22 inherited props, Spectrum `Card`’s 12 props through an exported cast, and shadcn’s 1,154 Next ambient augmentation props plus 6 Radix props. The 22 shadcn props from a falsely detected `GET` handler are addressed by #209. Mantine’s local generic alias resolution is the next highest impact structural slice.
Let's keep tackling the broader gap work. We'll need to drill down on the score/confidence experiment after we close the gaps I think

I’ll tackle the largest structural gap first: Mantine’s 66 missing `component` and `renderRoot` props. I’ll reproduce the failure in a focused fixture, trace where the factory’s result type stops resolving, and check the fix against the pinned corpora before opening another stacked PR. I’ll leave the confidence score experiment as a baseline for now.

+# 0021. Publish the semantic backend crates with the CLI
+
+**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-25
+
+## Context
+
+The 0.6.0 release published `caliper-docgen-core`, then Cargo rejected `caliper-docgen` because its `caliper-docgen-semantic` dependency had only a local path. Both the semantic backend and its `caliper-docgen-tsc-client` dependency were marked `publish = false`. ADR 0007 requires the backend in every CLI build, with activation controlled at runtime, so the published CLI also needs both crates from crates.io.
+
+## Decision
+
+Publish `caliper-docgen-tsc-client` and `caliper-docgen-semantic` as separate crates. Every path dependency in their chain and in `caliper-docgen` has a version requirement. Callisto includes the two crates as crates.io release packages so it can publish them before the CLI. The backend remains off at runtime unless requested.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- Cargo can package the CLI from registry dependencies, and Callisto can order the transport, backend and CLI publications by dependency.
+- The two backend crates become public distributions whose versions and API compatibility need release maintenance.
+- The failed 0.6.0 release commit cannot be repaired by rerunning its immutable source; a new release must include these manifest changes.
+
+## Alternatives considered
+
+- Move the backend and transport code into the CLI crate. That removes the registry dependencies but collapses two existing crate boundaries and makes the CLI own the process transport.
+- Exclude the backend from the published CLI. That would make the binary depend on how it was built, reversing ADR 0007's always-compiled contract.

content.text: The failing job is `Changesets`; the aggregate `CI` job fails because it depends on it. Callisto reports E176 during release simulation and shows the failed registry lookup for `caliper-docgen@0.6.0`. I reproduced that lookup outside the workspace. The remaining checks on #221 pass, but no edit to #221’s manifests can make the missing registry version appear.

You’re right. I checked the failed job, and **#221 does not fix CI**.

- `Changesets` fails with Callisto E176. Its log shows a lookup for `caliper-docgen@0.6.0` that returns “could not find”; the aggregate `CI` job then fails. The other #221 checks pass. [Failing job](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/actions/runs/40265446478/job/121386736233)
- The [0.6.0 release](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/actions/runs/40261575594) published **core**, then stopped at the CLI’s path-only dependency. CLI 0.6.0 is absent from crates.io, and the npm CLI, NAPI, and Storybook packages remain at 0.5.0. #201 and #202 hit the same Changesets failure.
- #221 would also publish the backend crates’ test helper binaries. I missed that, and it makes the PR unsuitable as written.

I’ve kept #221 **draft**. Rerunning the old release cannot fix its manifest, and weakening the CI check would conceal the incomplete release. The next repair depends on whether we keep `cargo install caliper-docgen`: that means either packaging the backend inside the CLI or publishing its two dependencies, followed by a deliberate recovery of the missing release. I’ve asked for that distribution choice; I have not published anything.

We use headings, bullets, etc right? Consider that these are added to generated changelogs, we want them to be friendly and scanable there.

I’ll review the pending changesets as release notes, shorten the ones that read like implementation reports, and keep the user-facing result easy to scan. I’m using the changeset workflow to check release impact and wording.
